CRLoMTL: Conflict-Resolution through Low-rank matrices for Multi-Task Learning

Ahmed Agiza*    Tasneem ShaffeeRahil BadkulSherief RedaSchool of EngineeringBrown UniversityProvidence, RI, USAahmed_agiza@brown.edu  tasneem_shaffee@brown.edu  rahil_badkul@brown.edu  sherief_reda@brown.edu
Abstract

Multi-task learning (MTL) improves model efficiency by sharing representations across related vision tasks, but it often suffers from negative transfer when task updates interfere with one another. Existing conflict-mitigation methods typically operate in gradient space, requiring explicit task-gradient manipulation and additional optimization steps. We propose Conflict-Resolution through Low-Rank Matrices for Multi-Task Learning (CRLoMTL), a parameter-efficient framework that mitigates task interference in the low-rank parameter-update space. CRLoMTL learns task-specific LoRA updates through task-specific passes, where each task updates its own low-rank matrices, and integrates these updates through global shared-subspace fusion. Specifically, we introduce a shared-subspace resolver based on singular value decomposition (SVD), referred to as the SVD resolver, which extracts a common low-dimensional orthonormal basis across task adapters and projects task updates into this shared space before merging them into a single deployment-time update. The resulting update can be folded into the backbone, preserving the inference structure of the original model without additional runtime branches. Experiments with Swin Transformer backbones on PASCAL-Context, NYUD-v2, and CelebA show that CRLoMTL achieves a favorable accuracy–parameter trade-off, improving over single-task baselines by up to 2.77% on PASCAL-Context, 5.03% on NYUD-v2, and 3.50% on CelebA, while training only a small fraction of the parameters used by single-task models.

1 Introduction

Multi-task learning (MTL) trains a single model to address multiple tasks by sharing intermediate representations and parameters. This paradigm improves sample efficiency through cross-task knowledge transfer, reduces the cost of training separate task-specific models, and lowers memory use and FLOPs by reusing a common backbone [1, 2]. MTL has shown strong utility across computer vision and natural language processing, where multiple related objectives can benefit from shared representations [3, 4].

Despite these advantages, MTL often suffers from task interference or negative transfer, where optimizing one task degrades the performance of another  [5, 6]. A common source of interference is gradient conflict, which occurs when task gradients point in opposing directions. Such conflicts can slow convergence, destabilize training, and bias the shared model toward tasks with dominant or easier objectives. Existing methods mitigate this issue through loss re-weighting [7], gradient projection or surgery [5, 6, 8], and adaptive multi-objective optimization [9, 10, 11]. However, these approaches often require task-wise gradient computation, optimization subproblems, or additional training-time mechanisms.

Low-rank adaptation provides an alternative way to model task-specific updates efficiently in parameter space. Instead of directly manipulating task gradients, low-rank matrices can isolate task-specific adaptation directions while keeping the shared backbone frozen. This motivates CRLoMTL, a parameter-efficient MTL framework that mitigates task interference by learning task-specific low-rank updates and fusing them into a unified model.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a multi-pass training strategy that alternates between task-specific passes and global passes. Task-specific passes learn separate low-rank adaptation matrices for each task, while global passes construct a fused update by resolving task-specific adapters through a common low-rank subspace.

  • •

    Unlike gradient-manipulation methods, CRLoMTL addresses negative transfer through low-rank parameter-space adaptation, producing a single fused update that can be merged into the backbone for inference without task-specific adapter selection or runtime fusion.

  • •

    We devise a shared-subspace fusion rule that extracts a low-dimensional orthonormal basis common to task-specific LoRA matrices and synthesizes a fused update through a closed-form least-squares projection.

  • •

    We evaluate CRLoMTL using Swin Transformer backbones on multiple MTL benchmarks, demonstrating a favorable accuracy–parameter trade-off compared with existing MTL baselines.

CRLoMTL balances task-specific adaptation with global shared-update construction, improving overall multi-task performance while using substantially fewer trainable parameters than existing MTL baselines and maintaining practical training-time and memory overhead. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We discuss background and related work in Section 2, introduce CRLoMTL in Section 3, present experiments in Section 4, and conclude in Section 5.

2 Background & Related Work

2.1 Multi-task Learning & Challenges

Multi-task learning (MTL) trains a single model to solve multiple related tasks by sharing representations, often improving knowledge transfer and reducing the cost of training separate task-specific models [1, 2]. Given a model f⁡(x,θ)f(x;\theta) and TT task losses {Lt}t=1T\{L_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, the standard MTL objective minimizes a weighted sum of task losses:

L⁡(θ)=∑t=1Twt​Lt​(f⁡(x,θ)),L(\theta)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}L_{t}(f(x;\theta)), (1)

where wtw_{t} controls the contribution of task tt. MTL has been widely used in computer vision, natural language processing, and healthcare  [12, 4, 13].

Despite these benefits, MTL can suffer from negative transfer, where sharing representations degrades one or more tasks [14]. This can arise from task imbalance, differences in task difficulty or data scale, and conflicting optimization directions [15]. A common indicator of task conflict is a negative inner product between task gradients:

⟨∇θLi​(θ),∇θLj​(θ)⟩<0,\langle\nabla_{\theta}L_{i}(\theta),\nabla_{\theta}L_{j}(\theta)\rangle<0, (2)

where ∇θLi​(θ)\nabla_{\theta}L_{i}(\theta) and ∇θLj​(θ)\nabla_{\theta}L_{j}(\theta) denote gradients from tasks ii and jj, respectively. Such conflicts can slow convergence, destabilize training, and degrade task performance [6]. In addition, MTL performance depends strongly on architectural choices, such as which layers to share and where to introduce task-specific components  [3, 9].

2.2 Gradient-Based Methodologies

Gradient-based MTL methods aim to reduce negative transfer by modifying task gradients or adaptively weighting task objectives. PCGrad [6] projects conflicting task gradients when their dot product is negative, while CAGrad [10] searches for a conflict-averse update direction that balances task improvement with proximity to the average gradient. MGDA [16] formulates MTL as multi-objective optimization and computes a common descent direction toward Pareto-optimal solutions. Other methods focus on balancing task learning dynamics: GradNorm [15] adjusts task weights based on relative training rates, DWA [17] uses recent loss-change ratios to assign dynamic weights, IMTL-G [18] balances gradient magnitudes and directions to avoid task dominance, and FAMO [11] provides an efficient adaptive optimization strategy with constant memory and computational overhead. Recent methods further consider fairness, alignment, and consistency across tasks. Nash-MTL [19] casts MTL as a bargaining game to obtain a balanced shared update direction. FairGrad [20] promotes fair resource allocation among tasks, while Go4Align [21] improves task alignment through group optimization. ConsMTL [22] highlights the importance of task-specific parameters for consistent multi-task optimization. Although these methods mitigate gradient conflict and task imbalance, they often introduce additional computational cost through task-wise gradient computation, optimization subproblems, or auxiliary balancing mechanisms, making efficiency a key challenge for scalable MTL.

2.3 Architectural Approaches

Beyond gradient-based optimization, several works address MTL challenges through architectural design, aiming to balance shared representations with task-specific adaptation. PAD-Net [23] promotes cross-task information flow by using auxiliary task predictions as intermediate representations for final task prediction. MTI-Net [24] extends this idea with multi-scale feature fusion and task-specific refinement modules, enabling interactions across tasks and scales. Other methods, such as AdaShare [25], learn adaptive sharing policies to determine which layers should be shared across tasks. Recently, transformer-based MTL architectures have gained increasing attention [26, 27]. InvPT [26] introduces task-specific inverted bottleneck modules on top of a shared transformer backbone, while MTLoRA [28] leverages low-rank matrices to model task interactions efficiently. RobuMTL [29] extends this direction to robust MTL by dynamically selecting and fusing perturbation-specific hierarchical LoRA experts under adverse weather conditions. Although these architectures can capture complex task relationships, many require additional parameters, task-specific branches, or extra inference-time modules [24, 23, 28], which may increase computational overhead. Moreover, understanding when MTL is beneficial and how to quantify task relatedness remains an active research direction [30].

2.4 Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and Model Merging

Recent advancements in Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques have shown promise in adapting large pre-trained models to specific tasks with minimal computational overhead. Among these techniques, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [31, 32] has gained significant attention due to its simplicity and effectiveness. LoRA introduces task-specific low-rank matrices to adapt pre-trained model weights. For a pre-trained weight matrix W∈ℝd×kW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}, LoRA defines the adapted weight as:

W′=W+B​A,W^{\prime}=W+BA, (3)

where B∈ℝd×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} and A∈ℝr×kA\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k} are low-rank matrices (typically r≪min⁡(d,k)r\ll\min(d,k)). During fine-tuning, only AA and BB are updated, significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters. PEFT methods like LoRA offer several advantages in terms of efficiency and flexibility. They require far less memory than full fine-tuning, as most model parameters remain frozen. Training is faster due to the reduced number of trainable parameters. Additionally, multiple task-specific adaptations can be stored and switched easily without modifying the base model. These characteristics make PEFT techniques particularly attractive for MTL scenarios, where they can potentially capture task-specific information efficiently while maintaining a shared base model.

LoRA and Model Merging.

Task arithmetic [33], TIES-Merging [34], and KnOTS [35] combine independently fine-tuned task models or adapters in parameter space, primarily as post-hoc merging procedures. Their evaluations largely consider experts with compatible prediction interfaces, such as models trained on different classification datasets, whereas CRLoMTL targets heterogeneous dense MTL, where tasks coexist within the same model but differ in output spaces, losses, and evaluation metrics. More importantly, CRLoMTL performs recurrent differentiable fusion during training: after the task-specific updates of each mini-batch, the resolver constructs a fused adapter whose global MTL loss backpropagates to the task adapters. Thus, the key distinction is training-time repeated fusion for heterogeneous MTL rather than one-time post-hoc model merging.

2.5 Problem Formulation

In this section, we formally define the MTL problem and introduce the notation used throughout the paper. Let 𝒟={(xi,yi1,…,yiT)}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i}^{1},...,y_{i}^{T})\}_{i=1}^{N} be a dataset of NN samples, where xi∈𝒳x_{i}\in\mathcal{X} represents the input features and yit∈𝒴ty_{i}^{t}\in\mathcal{Y}^{t} is the corresponding label for task t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,...,T\}. We consider a shared model fθ:𝒳→𝒴1×…×𝒴Tf_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}^{1}\times...\times\mathcal{Y}^{T} with parameters θ\theta, which aims to learn TT tasks simultaneously. For each task tt, we define a task-specific loss function ℒt:𝒴t×𝒴t→ℝ\mathcal{L}_{t}:\mathcal{Y}^{t}\times\mathcal{Y}^{t}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} that measures the discrepancy between the predicted output and the ground truth. The MTL objective can then be formulated as:

min⁡∑t=1Tθ⁡wt​1N​∑i=1Nℒt​(fθt​(xi),yit),\min_{\theta}\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{t}(f_{\theta}^{t}(x_{i}),y_{i}^{t}), (4)

where wt>0w_{t}>0 is the weight assigned to task tt, and fθt​(x)f_{\theta}^{t}(x) denotes the output of the model for task tt given input xx. The gradient of the overall loss with respect to the model parameters θ\theta is given by:

∇θℒ​(θ)=∑t=1Twt​∇θℒt​(θ),\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta), (5)

where ∇θℒt​(θ)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{t}(\theta) is the gradient of the loss for task tt. As discussed earlier, gradient conflicts occur when the gradients from different tasks point in opposing directions, as described in Equation 2. The primary challenge in MTL is finding a set of parameters θ\theta that performs well across all tasks, even in the presence of conflicting gradients. This involves balancing the potentially competing objectives of different tasks and finding a compromise that leads to good overall performance. Hence, our proposed framework attempts to leverage task-specific low-rank matrices to adapt the model parameters for each task and find an effective shared representation for all the tasks.

3 Methodology

CRLoMTL addresses multi-task learning challenges through low-rank matrix adaptations that operate directly on the model’s parameter space. As illustrated in Figure 1, our framework employs a multi-pass training mechanism that alternates between task-specific parameter updates and global shared-representation learning. This design enables the simultaneous capture of task-specific features and shared knowledge through three key components: (1) adaptive low-rank decomposition for task specialization, (2) task-specific passes that reduce direct gradient interference, and (3) global shared-subspace fusion that constructs a conflict-aware fused update.

3.1 Low-Rank Task Adaptation

For each task t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, we implement parameter adaptation through learnable low-rank matrices:

Wℓ,t=Wℓ+Bℓ,t​Aℓ,t,W_{\ell,t}=W_{\ell}+{B_{\ell,t}A_{\ell,t}}, (6)

where Wℓ∈ℝd×kW_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} denotes a frozen backbone weight matrix at LoRA-equipped layer ℓ\ell, and Bℓ,t∈ℝd×rB_{\ell,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} and Aℓ,t∈ℝr×kA_{\ell,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k} are the task-specific low-rank adaptation matrices for task tt, with r≪min⁡(d,k)r\ll\min(d,k). These low-rank components are inserted at selected adaptation points, providing task-specific adaptation while keeping the backbone frozen. Factorization reduces trainable parameters while retaining sufficient expressivity for task specialization.

3.2 Multi-Pass Training with Shared-Subspace Fusion

CRLoMTL performs alternating optimization within each mini-batch: the TT task adapters are updated sequentially and independently during the task-specific passes, with gradients cleared between tasks so their gradients are not explicitly combined. The updated adapters are then passed to the SVD resolver to construct a fused adapter, followed by one global pass using the aggregate MTL loss. Since the fused adapter remains differentiably connected to the persistent task adapters, the global loss backpropagates through the resolver and updates all task adapters; the adapters are neither overwritten nor reset. Thus, each cycle consists of TT task-specific updates followed by one global fused update.

3.2.1 Task-Specific Passes

During task-specific passes, each task tt independently updates its own layer-wise low-rank matrices {Aℓ,t,Bℓ,t}ℓ∈ℒ\{A_{\ell,t},B_{\ell,t}\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}. In these passes, the forward computation for each task incorporates both the frozen backbone and its task-specific parameters. Specifically, for a given task tt, each LoRA-equipped layer ℓ∈ℒ\ell\in\mathcal{L} uses the task-specific adapted weight defined in Eq. (6) during the forward pass, where WℓW_{\ell} denotes the frozen backbone weight matrix at layer ℓ\ell. In the backward pass, only the task-specific LoRA parameters {Aℓ,t,Bℓ,t}ℓ∈ℒ\{A_{\ell,t},B_{\ell,t}\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}} for the current task tt are updated. Crucially, the frozen backbone weights {Wℓ}ℓ∈ℒ\{W_{\ell}\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}} and the low-rank matrices of all other tasks {Aℓ,j,Bℓ,j}ℓ∈ℒ\{A_{\ell,j},B_{\ell,j}\}_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}} for j≠tj\neq t remain unchanged during this process. The adapters of other tasks are not used in the forward pass for task tt and are not updated during backpropagation. Gradients are cleared between task-specific passes, preventing explicit accumulation or combination of gradients across tasks. This design enables each task to learn task-specific adaptation directions while reducing direct gradient interference, since only the LoRA parameters of the current task are updated during its task-specific pass.

3.2.2 Global Passes

In the global passes (shown in Figure 1), CRLoMTL constructs a unified representation from the task-specific low-rank adapters using shared-subspace fusion. Given the current task-specific adapters {Aℓ,t,Bℓ,t}t=1T\{A_{\ell,t},B_{\ell,t}\}_{t=1}^{T} at each LoRA-equipped layer ℓ\ell, the global pass computes a shared basis using the resolver described in Section 3.3. Each task update is then projected onto this basis and aggregated to obtain a single fused low-rank update:

Wℓ,unified=Wℓ+𝐁ℓ,shared​𝐀ℓ,shared.W_{\ell,\mathrm{unified}}=W_{\ell}+\mathbf{B}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}. (7)

After all TT task-specific updates in the current mini-batch, the fused adapter is used for one task-agnostic forward pass with the aggregate MTL loss. Because the fused update remains differentiably connected to the persistent task adapters, the global backward pass propagates through the resolver and updates all task-specific adapters; they are neither overwritten nor reset.

The global pass acts as a conflict-aware consolidation step. While task-specific passes allow each task to learn specialized adaptation directions, the global pass merges these directions through a common low-dimensional subspace. This encourages the fused update to retain directions shared across tasks while reducing the influence of residual task-specific or conflicting components. After training, the resulting low-rank update is folded into the corresponding backbone weights, so the deployed model uses a single merged weight matrix without additional adapter branches or runtime fusion operations.

3.3 SVD-Based Shared-Subspace Resolver

The global pass in Section 3.2.2 requires a structured fusion mechanism for constructing a fused update from task-specific low-rank adapters. Directly averaging task-specific updates in the original parameter space may preserve task-specific or conflicting directions. We therefore introduce the SVD resolver, which uses truncated SVD to identify a common subspace for all tasks and then projects updates onto this basis via a least-squares solution. Let {Aℓ,t∈ℝr×dℓin,Bℓ,t∈ℝdℓout×r}t=1T\{A_{\ell,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{\ell}^{\mathrm{in}}},B_{\ell,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}^{\mathrm{out}}\times r}\}_{t=1}^{T} be the task-specific low-rank adapters learned at a LoRA-equipped layer ℓ∈ℒ\ell\in\mathcal{L}. The resolver is applied independently at each LoRA-equipped layer. We use Aℓ,tA_{\ell,t} for the shared input-side subspace of Δ​Wℓ,t=Bℓ,t​Aℓ,t\Delta W_{\ell,t}=B_{\ell,t}A_{\ell,t}, while Bℓ,tB_{\ell,t} retains task-dependent output mappings; BB-based extraction reduces the average relative improvement metric Δm\Delta_{m} (defined in Eq. (14)) by 0.030.03 percentage points. We concatenate the transposed AA matrices as

𝐀ℓ,cat=[Aℓ,1⊤|Aℓ,2⊤​|…|​Aℓ,T⊤]∈ℝdℓin×T​r.\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{cat}}=\bigl[A_{\ell,1}^{\top}\;|\;A_{\ell,2}^{\top}\;|\;\dots\;|\;A_{\ell,T}^{\top}\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}^{\mathrm{in}}\times Tr}. (8)

We use the learned Aℓ,tA_{\ell,t} directly without additional normalization; Frobenius normalization changes Δm\Delta_{m} by only 0.0010.001 percentage points, indicating negligible sensitivity to adapter magnitude.

Basis extraction.

Applying the truncated SVD 𝐀ℓ,cat=𝐔ℓ​𝚺ℓ​𝐕ℓ⊤\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{cat}}=\mathbf{U}_{\ell}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}\mathbf{V}_{\ell}^{\top} and retaining the leading rsr_{s} left singular vectors yields

𝐔ℓ,s\displaystyle\mathbf{U}_{\ell,s} =𝐔ℓ[:,1:rs],\displaystyle=\mathbf{U}_{\ell}[:,1:r_{s}], (9)
𝐀ℓ,shared\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}} =𝐔ℓ,s⊤∈ℝrs×dℓin,\displaystyle=\mathbf{U}_{\ell,s}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{s}\times d_{\ell}^{\mathrm{in}}},
rs\displaystyle r_{s} =min⁡(max⁡(1,⌊r/2⌋),dℓin).\displaystyle=\min(\max(1,\lfloor r/2\rfloor),\,d_{\ell}^{\mathrm{in}}).

Since 𝐔ℓ,s\mathbf{U}_{\ell,s} has orthonormal columns, 𝐀ℓ,shared\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}} has orthonormal rows.

Projection and aggregation.

For each task, we first define the task-specific LoRA update at layer ℓ\ell as

Δ​Wℓ,t=Bℓ,t​Aℓ,t.\Delta W_{\ell,t}=B_{\ell,t}A_{\ell,t}. (10)

We then project this update onto the shared basis using least squares:

𝐗ℓ,t=arg⁡min𝐗∈ℝdℓout×rs​‖Δ​Wℓ,t−𝐗𝐀ℓ,shared‖F2=Δ​Wℓ,t​𝐀ℓ,shared⊤,\mathbf{X}_{\ell,t}=\underset{\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}^{\mathrm{out}}\times r_{s}}}{\arg\min}\;\left\|\Delta W_{\ell,t}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}\right\|_{F}^{2}=\Delta W_{\ell,t}\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}^{\top}, (11)

where the closed form follows from the orthonormality of 𝐀ℓ,shared\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}, i.e., 𝐀ℓ,shared​𝐀ℓ,shared⊤=𝐈\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}^{\top}=\mathbf{I}. The fused adapter at layer ℓ\ell is then

𝐁ℓ,shared\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}} =1T​∑t=1T𝐗ℓ,t,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{X}_{\ell,t}, (12)
Wℓ,unified\displaystyle W_{\ell,\mathrm{unified}} =Wℓ+𝐁ℓ,shared​𝐀ℓ,shared.\displaystyle=W_{\ell}+\mathbf{B}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}}.

The global loss backpropagates through the resolver to all task-specific LoRA parameters. After training, the fused update is folded into the backbone, adding no inference overhead. The complete shared-subspace resolution procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1.

4 Experimental Results

4.1 Setup

We implement CRLoMTL in PyTorch and will release the code and pretrained weights upon publication. All experiments use a Swin Transformer backbone [36], pre-trained on ImageNet-1K [37], as the shared encoder. For dense prediction, we attach simple task-specific decoders for different dense tasks, similar to the one in HR-Net [38], which includes linear and bilinear upsampling layers. We use LoRA rank r=8r=8 with scaling α/r=2\alpha/r=2 (α=16\alpha=16). We evaluate our method primarily on two standard multi-task scene understanding benchmarks: PASCAL-Context [39] and NYUD-v2 [40]. Following common practice in MTL literature [24, 17], we use the standard PASCAL-Context split of 4,998 training and 5,105 validation images, with annotations for semantic segmentation, human-part segmentation, surface normal estimation, and saliency detection. For NYUD-v2, we use the standard split of 795 training and 654 testing images and evaluate semantic segmentation and depth estimation. For the dense prediction benchmarks, decoder parameters account for only 7%7\% of the total trainable parameters when Swin-Tiny is used as the backbone.

In addition, we evaluate CRLoMTL on CelebA [41], an image-level multi-attribute classification benchmark with over 200K face images and 40 binary facial attributes, which we treat as 40 binary classification tasks. This experiment assesses whether CRLoMTL extends beyond dense scene understanding to many-task classification. To train our MTL model, we use a weighted sum of task losses:

LossMTL=∑i=1Tωtask ​i​Ltask ​i,\text{Loss}_{\text{MTL}}=\sum_{i=1}^{T}\omega_{\text{task }i}L_{\text{task }i}, (13)

where ωtask ​i\omega_{\text{task }i} and Ltask ​iL_{\text{task }i} denote the weight and loss for task ii, respectively. For PASCAL-Context and NYUD-v2, we use pixel-wise cross-entropy for semantic and human-part segmentation, balanced binary cross-entropy for saliency, and L1L_{1} loss for surface normals and depth estimation. We adopt the task weights used by Vandenhende et al. [24]. For CelebA, we use binary cross-entropy over the 40 image-level facial attribute classification tasks. Accuracy experiments were conducted on a V100, while efficiency profiling was conducted on an H100 under a controlled setup using batch size 32. For the dense prediction experiments, all methods use AdamW with cosine decay, weight decay 0.050.05, batch size 3232, and 500500 epochs, with 448×448448\times 448 inputs for dense prediction and 224×224224\times 224 for CelebA.

4.2 Baseline Methods

We compare CRLoMTL with representative state-of-the-art (SOTA) MTL methods from five categories: task-interaction architectures, parameter-efficient adaptation, dynamic loss weighting, gradient-balancing optimization, and parameter-space merging controls. These include MTI-Net [24], MTLoRA [28], DWA [17], PCGrad [6], CAGrad [10], Nash-MTL [19], MGDA [16], IMTL-G [18], FAMO [11], FairGrad [20], Go4Align [21], and ConsMTL [22]. We additionally include Shared-LoRA and a KnOTS-style SVD merging control [35] to isolate the benefit of CRLoMTL’s recurrent training-time fusion over shared adaptation and post-hoc-style LoRA merging. All methods are implemented within the same experimental framework using the same backbone and datasets, with only the MTL or adapter-fusion strategy varied.

4.3 Evaluation Results on PASCAL-Context

We use mean intersection over union (mIoU) to evaluate semantic segmentation, saliency estimation, and human part segmentation. For the surface normal task, we use the root-mean-square error (RMSE) in the predicted angles. To measure overall performance, we use Δm\Delta_{m}, which is the average per-task improvement in performance compared to the single-task baseline:

Δm=1T​∑i=1T(−1)li​(Mi−Ms​t,i)Ms​t,i,\Delta_{m}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^{T}(-1)^{l_{i}}\frac{(M_{i}-M_{st,i})}{M_{st,i}}, (14)

where li=1l_{i}=1 if a lower value means better for performance measure MiM_{i} of task ii, and 0 otherwise. Single-task performance is measured for a fully converged model using the same backbone network only for that task. Tables 1 and 2 present the results for models using Swin-Tiny and Swin-Small backbones, respectively. We compare CRLoMTL against existing SOTA MTL methods and single-task baselines. The reported parameter counts refer to trainable parameters during training. As shown in Table 1, CRLoMTL improves the single-task baseline by 2.77%2.77\% while training only 4% of the parameters when using a Swin-Tiny backbone, demonstrating a favorable trade-off between accuracy and parameter efficiency. On the larger Swin-Small backbone (Table 2), CRLoMTL delivers a 6.08% gain while training less than 6% of the parameters, demonstrating that its effectiveness is maintained as model capacity increases. Additionally, unlike methods that retain task-specific branches or adapters at inference, such as MTI-Net [24] and MTLoRA [28], CRLoMTL folds the fused low-rank update into the backbone after training, yielding a single deployed model without task-specific adapter branches. The default single-seed result reported in Table 1 is Δm=2.77%\Delta_{m}=2.77\%. Across three random seeds, CRLoMTL obtains Δm=2.74±0.03%\Delta_{m}=2.74\pm 0.03\%; detailed per-task results are provided in the supplementary material.

4.3.1 Analysis of Global Pass

To assess the effect of the global pass, we analyze update alignment in the low-rank parameter space. Using the task-specific LoRA updates Δ​Wℓ,t\Delta W_{\ell,t} defined in Eq. (10), we measure their change over one training cycle as

δℓ,t=Δ​Wℓ,t(after)−Δ​Wℓ,t(before).\delta_{\ell,t}=\Delta W_{\ell,t}^{(\mathrm{after})}-\Delta W_{\ell,t}^{(\mathrm{before})}. (15)

For full CRLoMTL, “after” is measured after the task-specific and global passes; for the no-global-pass ablation, it is measured after the task-specific passes only. We flatten the analyzed update changes into one vector per task and compute pairwise cosine similarity:

Ci​j=⟨δi,δj⟩‖δi‖2​‖δj‖2.C_{ij}=\frac{\langle\delta_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle}{\|\delta_{i}\|_{2}\|\delta_{j}\|_{2}}. (16)

We report the mean and minimum off-diagonal entries of CC as average and worst-case task-update alignment. Figure 2 shows that the global pass increases both alignment metrics, whereas the no-global-pass ablation remains near zero or slightly negative. This suggests that the global pass encourages more compatible task-specific LoRA updates before fusion, without using an explicit alignment loss.

4.3.2 Analysis of SVD Conflict Suppression

We analyze the SVD resolver in parameter-update space to assess how the SVD projection affects cross-task compatibility. For each LoRA-equipped layer ℓ\ell and task tt, we use the task-specific LoRA update Δ​Wℓ,t\Delta W_{\ell,t} defined in Eq. (10). Following the projection in Eq. (11), we decompose each update into a component retained in the shared subspace and an orthogonal residual:

𝐊ℓ,t=𝐗ℓ,t​𝐀ℓ,shared,𝐑ℓ,t=Δ​Wℓ,t−𝐊ℓ,t.\mathbf{K}_{\ell,t}=\mathbf{X}_{\ell,t}\mathbf{A}_{\ell,\mathrm{shared}},\qquad\mathbf{R}_{\ell,t}=\Delta W_{\ell,t}-\mathbf{K}_{\ell,t}. (17)

The retained component 𝐊ℓ,t\mathbf{K}_{\ell,t} captures the portion of the task update represented by the SVD-derived shared basis at layer ℓ\ell, whereas 𝐑ℓ,t\mathbf{R}_{\ell,t} corresponds to the component discarded by the projection. We quantify cross-task compatibility using the average pairwise cosine similarity and the negative-pair rate (NPR), defined as the fraction of task pairs with negative cosine similarity, over the sets {Δ​Wℓ,t}\{\Delta W_{\ell,t}\}, {𝐊ℓ,t}\{\mathbf{K}_{\ell,t}\}, and {𝐑ℓ,t}\{\mathbf{R}_{\ell,t}\}.

As shown in Figure 3(a), the retained components 𝐊ℓ,t\mathbf{K}_{\ell,t} consistently achieve higher pairwise cosine similarity than both the original updates Δ​Wℓ,t\Delta W_{\ell,t} and the residuals 𝐑ℓ,t\mathbf{R}_{\ell,t}, indicating stronger alignment within the recovered shared subspace. Figure 3(b) further shows that 𝐊ℓ,t\mathbf{K}_{\ell,t} has a substantially lower NPR, while the residuals exhibit the highest NPR. This suggests that the SVD projection concentrates cross-task-compatible directions in the retained component and relegates less compatible, task-specific directions to the residual. Finally, Figure 3(c) shows that the fused LoRA update is more strongly aligned with 𝐊ℓ,t\mathbf{K}_{\ell,t} than with 𝐑ℓ,t\mathbf{R}_{\ell,t}, indicating that the final fused adapter is primarily guided by the shared SVD-retained subspace. Additional retained/residual energy analysis is provided in the supplementary material.

4.3.3 Efficiency Analysis

For efficiency analysis, we evaluate all methods on the same NVIDIA H100 GPU under an identical PASCAL setup. As shown in Figure 4, CRLoMTL has a 14.35 GB memory footprint, within 6% of the lowest baseline footprint (13.56 GB), while benefiting from its parameter-efficient low-rank updates. Its average training time is 2.79 min/epoch, with most of the overhead coming from the alternating multi-pass procedure: task-specific passes account for 46.22% of the step time, the global backward pass and gradient scaling account for 33.30%, and global fusion accounts for only 20.05%. Thus, the main training cost comes from multi-pass optimization rather than the SVD-based fusion itself.

As shown in Table 3, merging reduces CRLoMTL from 31.91M to 29.47M parameters, matching vanilla MTL, with comparable evaluation time (229.23±2.64229.23\pm 2.64s vs. 230.63±2.40230.63\pm 2.40s). Before merging, only 4.39M parameters are trainable (2.44M encoder LoRA parameters and 1.95M task-specific decoder parameters), while the folded adapters introduce no inference-time branches or runtime fusion.

4.4 Evaluation Results on NYUD-v2

We evaluate CRLoMTL on NYUD-v2 [40], an indoor scene understanding benchmark with semantic segmentation and depth estimation, using mIoU and RMSE, respectively. As shown in Table 4, CRLoMTL improves the single-task baseline by 5.03%5.03\% with only 2.22M trainable parameters, corresponding to 3.96% of the single-task and 7.79% of the standard MTL parameter counts.

4.5 Additional Evaluation on CelebA

We further evaluate CRLoMTL on CelebA [41], a many-task image-level classification benchmark with 40 tasks. To improve scalability, we retain 40 task-specific classification heads but share LoRA adapters within 7 manually defined semantic groups: hair, facial hair, expression, makeup, accessories, face shape, and identity/style. The grouping is determined solely by attribute semantics.

Grouping and scalability.

Using 40 per-attribute adapters improves Δm\Delta_{m} from +3.50%+3.50\% to +4.31%+4.31\% but increases task passes and resolver inputs. In this setting, SVD accounts for only 8.18%8.18\% of epoch time, versus 45.43%45.43\% for task-specific passes and 34.62%34.62\% for the global backward.

Setup. Following ConsMTL [22], we train for 15 epochs and report MR and Δm\Delta_{m} from Eq. 14, where lower MR and higher Δm\Delta_{m} are better. CRLoMTL achieves the best overall result in Table 5.

4.6 Ablation Study

Shared Subspace Rank Sensitivity: Table 6(a) shows negligible sensitivity to rsr_{s}, with only 0.0060.006 percentage-point variation; we therefore use rs=r/2r_{s}=r/2 as a compact default.

CRLoMTL Components: Table 6(b) isolates task-specific adaptation and shared-subspace fusion. Shared-LoRA, a standard MTL model with one LoRA shared across tasks, shows that the gain is not due to LoRA regularization or backbone freezing alone. The SVD resolver further improves over average fusion with only training-time overhead and no inference cost after merging.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity: On PASCAL-Context, we vary LoRA rank with α=2​r\alpha=2r and α\alpha with fixed r=8r=8 (Table 6(c)–(d)). The small variation in Δm\Delta_{m} across tested ranks and nonzero α\alpha values indicates limited sensitivity to these hyperparameters.

5 Conclusion

CRLoMTL combines task-specific LoRA adaptation with shared-subspace fusion, achieving a favorable accuracy–parameter trade-off across three MTL benchmarks without inference-time overhead. Future work will explore larger task settings, other PEFT modules, and shared-subspace dynamics.

Supplementary Material for
CRLoMTL: Conflict-Resolution through Low-Rank Matrices for Multi-Task Learning

Appendix A Additional SVD Resolver Analysis

Retained and residual energy:

We additionally analyze the relative Frobenius energy of the retained component 𝐊ℓ,t\mathbf{K}_{\ell,t} and the residual 𝐑ℓ,t\mathbf{R}_{\ell,t}, as shown in Figure 5. The retained component does not necessarily contain the majority of the update energy; instead, it captures the portion of the task-specific update represented by the shared SVD basis. In contrast, the residual may contain a larger fraction of the energy, but it is substantially less compatible across tasks, as indicated by the NPR analysis in the main paper. This suggests that the resolver extracts a compact shared subspace while leaving larger task-specific variation in the residual.

Appendix B Additional Feature-Space Analysis

Beyond aggregate metrics, we compare the feature spaces induced by CRLoMTL and the vanilla MTL baseline. Using t-SNE projections and silhouette scores, we visualize how each method separates task-specific embeddings while preserving intra-task cohesion. This qualitative analysis highlights differences in feature compactness and cross-task interference that are not always apparent from scalar metrics alone.

Figure 6 shows t-SNE visualizations of task-specific features for MTL and CRLoMTL after 175 training epochs on PASCAL-Context. Both methods exhibit separable features across tasks; however, CRLoMTL produces more compact clusters per task, indicating stronger intra-task feature consistency. This observation is further supported by a higher silhouette score for CRLoMTL, reflecting improved cluster compactness and separation. In contrast, MTL shows elongated clusters, which may reflect feature noise or redundancy. The silhouette coefficient measures how well a data point is assigned to its cluster relative to other clusters [42].

Appendix C Additional Ablation and Stability Analysis

Table 7 provides the per-task variation across three random seeds. The small standard deviations for semantic segmentation, human parts, saliency, and surface normals show that the performance gains are not driven by a single task or a favorable initialization. The overall Δm=2.74±0.03%\Delta_{m}=2.74\pm 0.03\% further indicates that CRLoMTL maintains a consistent multi-task improvement across runs.

    Hair: Bald, Bangs, Black Hair, Blond Hair, Brown Hair, Gray Hair, Receding Hairline, Straight Hair, Wavy Hair.

    Facial hair: 5 o’Clock Shadow, Goatee, Mustache, No Beard, Sideburns.

  • •

    Expression: Smiling, Mouth Slightly Open, Narrow Eyes.

  • •

    Makeup: Arched Eyebrows, Bags Under Eyes, Heavy Makeup, Rosy Cheeks, Wearing Lipstick.

  • •

    Accessories: Eyeglasses, Wearing Earrings, Wearing Hat, Wearing Necklace, Wearing Necktie.

  • •

    Face shape: Attractive, Big Lips, Big Nose, Chubby, Double Chin, High Cheekbones, Oval Face, Pointy Nose, Pale Skin.
